quotes-go-quiet:
Many quotes don’t die of price. They die of silence. A quote goes out by email, the customer has one question about it, and the question arrives somewhere nobody connects to the quote: a text to the technician’s phone, a website chat at 9pm, a reply to an email address nobody checks. Meanwhile the office sends one “just checking in” email and moves on. The fix is an agent that follows up on every open quote across text, email, chat and phone, answers questions from the quote itself, books the next step, and stops the moment the customer replies or says no.

How the work runs today: two quotes that went quiet

Here is how quote follow-up usually runs at a small business that sells big-ticket jobs.

Step Who Where When
Quote written Technician, estimator or salesperson Field-service or quoting software, or the store’s system At the visit
Quote sent The software, automatically Email, as a PDF Same day
Follow-up Office manager or the salesperson Phone, email When someone remembers, usually once
Questions from the customer Whoever sees them first A personal phone, the website chat, a shared inbox Whenever they’re noticed
Quote closed out Office manager CRM or a spreadsheet Weeks later, marked “lost”

Now take two illustrative businesses in the same week: a heating and cooling company, and a furniture showroom that sells made-to-order sofas.

The heating and cooling company: a quote for a new furnace and AC

When Channel What happens
Tuesday, 6:10pm In person, then email The comfort advisor’s visit ends. The software emails a PDF with two options: $9,800 and $12,400. The homeowner says “we’ll talk it over tonight”.
Wednesday Nothing. The office’s follow-up list lives in the office manager’s head.
Friday, 11:00am Phone The office manager calls. Voicemail. She leaves a message asking him to call back.
Saturday, 9:30pm Website chat The homeowner asks: “Does the $9,800 option include a new thermostat?” The chat takes a name and email and promises a reply “within one business day”.
Monday, 10:40am Email Someone answers the chat question. The homeowner replies that they went with another company on Sunday.
Three weeks later CRM The quote is marked “lost: price”.

The furniture showroom: a quote for a custom sectional

When Channel What happens
Saturday, 3:00pm In store, then email A couple picks a sectional in the showroom. The salesperson emails a quote: $4,200, eight weeks to deliver.
Tuesday, 8:45pm Email They reply to the quote email: “Could we see the fabric in grey before we decide?” It lands in the salesperson’s inbox. She’s off until Thursday.
Thursday, 10:00am Email She replies with grey swatch photos and an invitation to come in.
Thursday, 4:30pm Email They thank her. They found something at another store on Wednesday.

Nobody in either story was careless, and the price wasn’t the problem. Both customers asked a question, and a question about a quote is a buyer telling you what stands between them and yes. The homeowner asked about a thermostat on a Saturday night through the website chat, which knew nothing about his quote. The couple asked about fabric on a Tuesday evening by replying to an email that only one person could see. In both cases the answer came a day and a half later, after someone else had answered first.

Why do quotes go quiet?

1. Follow-up depends on someone remembering. The quote goes out automatically. The follow-up doesn’t. It sits on a list in the office manager’s head, competing with today’s phone calls, so most quotes get one email or one call, and then nothing. The cost is every quote that would have closed with one more, better-timed message. You notice this when you can’t say, for last month’s quotes, how many were followed up at all.

2. The customer’s question lands somewhere that can’t see the quote. People answer on whatever channel is in front of them. A text to the technician’s phone, a website chat, a reply to the quote email, a voicemail to the main line. Each lands in a different place, and none of them knows which quote it’s about. So the question waits, or gets a general answer, while the customer is still deciding. You notice this when quotes are marked “lost” and nobody can find the last thing the customer asked.

3. “Just checking in” isn’t follow-up. A generic nudge asks the customer to do the work: dig out the PDF, remember what confused them, and write back. The messages that move a decision answer the thing they were stuck on, such as what each option includes, what the timeline is, or whether financing is available. And the follow-up has to stop when they say no. A business that keeps texting after “we went with someone else” doesn’t get the next job either. You notice this when your “lost” reasons say “price” but nobody ever discussed price.

no-shows:
Picture a dental patient who saw her reminder, couldn’t make it, and found that cancelling was harder than not turning up. The reminder came by SMS and only understood one reply. Rescheduling meant phoning during office hours. The email she sent went to an inbox nobody checks until mid-morning. So the chair sits empty, and the practice finds out at the appointment time. Tutoring centres lose trial-class seats the same way. The fix is an agent that confirms on whichever channel people answer, rebooks in your booking system, and offers the freed seat to your waitlist.

Replies checked Front desk coordinator The reminder tool’s inbox When there’s a gap between patients

Wednesday, 8:40pm Email The patient realises she has a meeting, and emails the office to ask for next week instead. It lands in the shared inbox.

Thursday, 9:00am The hygienist’s chair is empty for an hour. Her email is read at 11:20am.

The tutoring centre, 4:30pm trial class

When Channel What happens

Wednesday, 9:15pm SMS She texts the number on the centre’s flyer: “Can we do Saturday instead?” The number is the admin’s own phone, which is off for the evening.
Thursday, 4:30pm The teacher holds the class for a student who isn’t coming. The parent believes she has rescheduled.
Friday, 10:00am SMS The admin sees the message, replies with Saturday times, and gets no answer. The family has moved on.

Nobody in either story was careless. The patient tried twice. The parent asked politely. Both businesses sent reminders. Each seat was lost in the gap between the channel the business used and the channel the customer used. The dental reminder went out by SMS, and the patient answered by email. The centre printed a phone number on its flyer, and the parent texted it at an hour when nobody was holding that phone. In both cases the business did reach the customer, and the customer did reply. The reply just landed somewhere that couldn’t act on it until the seat was already gone.

Why do people no-show after a reminder?

1. Reminders talk, but they don’t listen. The reminder in our story is one text that understands one reply: “C”. A patient who replies “can I come at 4 instead?” gets no answer, because the reminder can’t do anything with that. A reply on a different channel goes nowhere at all. The cost is a seat that looked confirmed until it was empty. You notice this when your no-show list includes people who did try to get in touch.

2. Rescheduling is harder than not showing up. If changing an appointment means calling during office hours and waiting on hold, then for a busy person the easiest option is to do nothing. Every no-show costs the slot itself, and it may cost the next visit too, because someone who skipped once can feel awkward about booking again. You notice this when rescheduling requests arrive by email and text after hours and sit there until morning.

3. You find out at the appointment time. By 9:00am there’s no one to call into the chair, and by 4:30pm the trial class has started. A slot freed on Wednesday evening could have gone to someone on your waitlist. A slot discovered empty at the appointment time just goes to waste, and so does the hygienist’s or teacher’s hour you’re paying for anyway. You notice this when you have a waitlist and empty chairs on the same day.

What we’d build: confirm and rebook on the channel people answer

  • Someone can’t make it, on any channel, at any hour → Front desk agent → real times offered from your schedule, the appointment moved, and a confirmation on the same channel. The old slot is released at once.
  • A slot is released → Front desk agent → offered to your waitlist in the order you set. The first person to reply is booked into it.

speed-to-lead:
The expensive part of a lead is the wait after it arrives. A lead comes in by ad form, website form, chat, text or phone, then sits in an inbox, the CRM and someone’s to-do list. Hours later a rep calls, on a channel the lead never chose, and gets voicemail. Meanwhile the lead asked two other companies, and one replied at once. The fix is an agent that replies within a minute on the channel the lead used, asks your qualifying questions, books into the right calendar, and keeps following up across channels until the lead answers.

How the work runs today: one lead, three companies

Picture a homeowner, call her Maria. Her roof is leaking and she wants it looked at before the weekend. On her lunch break, between 12:41 and 12:47pm, she contacts three roofing companies from her phone, each in a different way.

12:41pm A Filled in the “Free estimate” form on a Facebook ad Nothing until 4:55pm, then a call while she was in a meeting. Voicemail.
12:44pm B Typed into the chat on their website “Leave your email and we’ll be in touch within 1 business day.”
12:47pm C Texted the number on their Google listing A reply within a minute, two questions, and a choice of Thursday 8am or Friday 4pm

Maria booked Friday 4pm with Company C at 12:52pm, from the same text thread, and went back to her lunch. Company C wasn’t bigger or cheaper. It answered on the channel she used, while she was still looking.

Assigned to the estimator for her area Office manager CRM 2 hours 10 minutes

Follow-up email Estimator Email Next morning
Third attempt Nobody Never

Nobody in that table was careless, and every one of them did their job. The lead still waited four hours for a first reply, on a channel she didn’t choose.

Why do leads go cold before anyone replies?

1. The lead waits in a queue before anyone talks to it. A form fill turns into an email, the email turns into a CRM record, the record gets assigned, and only then does someone reach out. Each handover is reasonable on its own. Together they add hours. When Harvard Business Review researchers studied how companies respond to online leads, their conclusion was blunt: “most companies are not responding nearly fast enough” (Oldroyd, McElheran and Elkington, HBR, March 2011). Every hour in that queue is an hour in which a competitor can reply first, and the ad money that bought the lead is already spent. You notice this when your CRM shows a first-contact time hours after the lead arrived.

2. You answer on the wrong channel. Maria typed on her phone during lunch. Company A called her at 4:55pm, in a meeting. Someone who chose to message may not be able to take a call right then, and a callback that lands in voicemail resets the clock. Each missed callback means another attempt, more rep time, and another chance for the lead to book elsewhere. The reply should come where the lead asked, and move to a call only when they want one. You notice this when reps say leads “never pick up”.

3. Follow-up stops at two. Company A tried one call and one email, then moved on. Leads go quiet for ordinary reasons: a meeting, a school run, a phone left in the car. Without a follow-up schedule that runs on its own, a lead that went quiet once is a lead that’s gone. You paid for every one of those leads, so a lead dropped after one call is ad spend written off, even when the person still needs the job done. You notice this when your CRM is full of leads marked “contacted, no response”.

There is a fourth, quieter cost. When Company A’s estimator finally called, he didn’t know which ad Maria had clicked or what the form said about the leak. She would have had to explain everything again. A rep who walks in knowing the leak, the photo and the ad starts the visit as the company that listened, which is a better start to any estimate.

This is the job of AtomsAI’s Sales agent. It answers new leads on every channel, with one memory, and acts inside your CRM and calendars.

  • Lead qualifies → Sales agent → books into the right person’s calendar (by territory, round robin or account owner), confirms by text, and sends the rep a brief.
  • Lead goes quiet → Sales agent → follows up on your schedule across channels, and stops the moment they reply or say no.

Why do after-hours messages go unanswered?

1. Every channel lands in its own inbox. Nobody sees all of it, so nobody can answer all of it, and the morning starts with someone hunting through each place in turn. You notice this when a customer says “I messaged you last night” and nobody can find the message.

2. Customers repeat themselves. The 6:42pm visitor came back at 11:48pm and asked the same question, because nothing remembered the first conversation. The 7:40pm caller tried again at 6:55am. When your team finally replies, different people answer different channels, sometimes with different answers. You notice this when two of your staff reply to the same customer in two places.

3. The first reply gets the first chance. Someone who needs help tonight may well ask more than one business. If the AC is out and the homeowner messages three companies, whichever answers first gets the first chance to book. A reply at 8:30am, however friendly, competes with someone who answered at 7:13pm. You notice this when a customer replies to your morning message with “Thanks, already sorted.”

This is the job of AtomsAI’s Front desk agent. In short:

  • After-hours message on any channel → Front desk agent → answered, booked, rescheduled or noted in your system, and confirmed on the channel the customer used.
  • Something urgent or outside its rules → Front desk agent → your on-call person paged with a summary, or a handover waiting for your team in the morning.

It answers every channel with one memory, so a customer who starts on chat and switches to a call is picking up the same conversation. When a new enquiry needs qualifying, for ex. a full system replacement rather than a repair, it works alongside the Sales agent. What you control. Which channels the agent answers, during which hours, and in whose name. What it can book, change or cancel, and what needs a person to approve. What leaving it costs

Here’s a worked example. Swap in your own numbers.

Take the same three-location home-services company, getting 20 contacts after 6pm on an average weeknight, across every channel.

  • Say 6 of those 20 are new people asking for a job or a visit.
  • Say the average first job is worth $400.
  • Say that, because they hear nothing until morning, 2 of the 6 book with someone else first.

That’s 2 × $400 = $800 a night. Across 22 weeknights a month, that’s $17,600 a month, before weekends and before what those customers would have spent with you next year.

Then there’s the morning. If the other 14 contacts each take 4 minutes to find, read and reply to, that’s 56 minutes of catch-up before the phones even start, every day.

You can measure your own version in a week. Count everything that arrives after closing, on every channel, and note how many were new customers and how many of those you actually booked.

You’ll leave knowing which conversations an agent can finish on its own, which ones need a person, and what it would take to connect your booking system and CRM.

the-demo-was-never-the-hard-part:
AI pilots usually stall before production because of what sits between the model’s output and a finished piece of work: writing back to your systems, approvals, the exceptions nobody scoped, and no agreed number for whether it’s working. Fix those, and the model is rarely the problem.

Stalled AI programmes tend to share a shape. A pilot that worked. A steering committee that approved. And, months later, nothing in production.

The post-mortem almost always blames the model, or “change management.” It’s usually neither. It’s the gap between producing an output and finishing a piece of work.

Where does the work actually end?

A demo ends when the model returns text. The work ends when the invoice is paid, the ticket is closed, the policy is bound. Between those two points sit the write-back to the system of record, the approval nobody had authority to design, the exception path for the documents that arrive malformed, the audit trail your controller needs at month-end, and someone on call when a downstream API returns 500 for an hour.

None of that is glamorous and all of it is the project. Integration is the product.

How do you know if it’s working?

The second reason is measurement. A pilot is judged by whether a room was impressed. Production is judged by whether it’s still trusted in month four — and if you can’t answer “is it working?” with a number, trust decays to zero on the first visible mistake. That’s why we write failure tests before the happy path (more on evals here): accuracy against a labelled set, cost per run against a ceiling, latency against a budget, and an alarm when any of them moves.

Which workflow should you automate first?

RFPs name the workflow that’s easiest to describe. The expensive one is the one people are slightly embarrassed about — the shared mailbox, the Friday spreadsheet, the queue with no owner. Look in the exception queue, not the process diagram.

If you want a cheap test of whether a pilot will survive: ask who owns the runbook, what the rollback is, and what number gets checked on Monday. If nobody can answer, the model quality is irrelevant.

Somewhere in your finance team, someone spends Friday fixing the invoices that failed OCR. Fix Friday.

See how we take a workflow from teardown to production, or what a document intake agent does with invoices that arrive malformed.

Questions buyers ask

Why do AI pilots fail to reach production? Rarely because of the model. They stall on the work between an output and a finished task: writing back to your systems, approvals, the exceptions nobody scoped, and no agreed number for whether it’s working.

How do you move an AI pilot into production? Scope the full workflow to the point where the work is finished, including write-backs, approvals and the exception path. Agree the numbers that define success before you build, and name who owns the runbook and the rollback.

Which workflow should we automate with AI first? Look in the exception queue, not the process diagram: the shared mailbox, the Friday spreadsheet, the queue with no owner. That is usually where the cost is.

How do you know if an AI system is working in production? Measure it against a labelled set for accuracy, a ceiling for cost per run and a budget for speed, with an alarm when any of them moves.
write-the-evals-before-the-prompt:
To test an AI agent before launch, build the eval set first: a labelled sample of real inputs and correct outcomes from the people who do the work today. It becomes the specification, gives you a pass rate instead of an opinion, and lets you set the threshold yourself. Then add tests for cost, bad input and drift.

Most teams build the thing, then try to measure it. That order is why so many systems get quietly switched off.

Why write the evals before the prompt?

An eval suite written first is a specification. Before we ingest a document or write a prompt, we sit with practitioners and collect the real inputs: the questions a support team gets asked most, recent exceptions from an AP mailbox, past underwriting decisions with their outcomes. Labelling that set is small work next to the build, and it decides the whole design. Sorting exceptions this way can show that most of them fall into a few mechanical buckets, which changes what gets built.

It also changes what “good” means. Without a labelled set, quality is whatever the last demo felt like. With one, you have a pass rate, and you can set the threshold yourself. That threshold belongs to the customer, not the vendor. A decision workflow may need a very high pass rate, while a drafting workflow that a person reviews can start lower. Both can be right, because the cost of being wrong is very different.

What should you test beyond accuracy?

Cost per run, with a ceiling. A system that works but costs more per item than the work it replaces is a system finance will kill. Put the ceiling in CI.

Malformed and adversarial input. Missing fields, wrong currencies, duplicate submissions, a document in an unexpected language. Each becomes a test and a documented behaviour.

Drift. Scores move — model updates, document changes, seasonal input shifts. An alarm on a moving score is what separates a system you trust from one you hope about.

Why do evals matter to the business?

The commercial argument matters more than the engineering one. A CXO cannot defend a system they can’t measure. Hand them a scoreboard — accuracy, cost, latency, per workflow, per month — and the conversation about expanding to the next workflow takes ten minutes.

Evals from day one. Not later.

The pass rate is also what decides how much an agent can do on its own; see how much autonomy an agent should have. For where evals sit in a build, see how we work.

Questions buyers ask

What is an AI eval? An eval is a test that scores an AI system’s output against known correct answers from your own work. A set of them, built from real inputs, tells you the pass rate before anything goes live.

How do you test an AI agent before launch? Collect a labelled set of real inputs from the team that does the work today, write the evals against it before writing prompts, and add tests for cost per run, malformed input and drift.

What accuracy should an AI agent have before launch? It depends on what a mistake costs, and you set the threshold, not the vendor. A decision workflow needs a much higher pass rate than a drafting workflow that a person reviews.

How do you measure AI accuracy after launch? Keep running the same evals and put an alarm on the score. Model updates, document changes and seasonal shifts all move it.
how-much-autonomy-should-an-agent-have:
An AI agent should have as much autonomy as its measured pass rate supports, and no more. Write down what it may not do without a person, express each limit as a number your business already uses, start tight, and loosen one limit at a time. Anything you can’t undo stays with a person.

“Should the agent do this on its own?” gets argued as a matter of principle. It’s a threshold, and thresholds are cheap to change if you build for it.

What should an AI agent never do without approval?

The first artifact we write for any agent is not a prompt or a tool list. It’s the list of things it is not allowed to do without a human. That list determines everything downstream: which credentials it gets, which writes are staged versus committed, what triggers a hold, what a rollback looks like.

Gates are best expressed as a number your business already understands. In accounts payable that might be a dollar amount: above your limit, a human approves with the extraction and the source document side by side; below it, the system commits and logs. In underwriting it might be confidence: below the line, route to a senior reviewer. Start conservative and loosen once the measured pass rate justifies it. Because the threshold is configuration, loosening it is a settings change, not a re-architecture.

How do you give an agent more autonomy safely?

A shadow lane. Run on production data, produce real outputs, commit nothing, for one to two weeks. Then compare the system’s decisions against your team’s. That comparison is what gets a workflow approved. It’s a far easier conversation than a debate about model capability.

Reversibility. Every action logged with inputs, reasoning and the identity that authorised it. Idempotent writes. Replay from any state. If you can’t undo an action, it doesn’t get automated yet, whatever the pass rate says.

What happens when the agent is confidently wrong?

One more thing worth designing early: what happens when the system is confidently wrong. Not “if” — confidently wrong is the normal failure mode. Who notices, how fast, what’s the blast radius, how do you undo it? Write that down before launch and test it before handover.

Autonomy isn’t a stance. It’s a dial, with an owner and a number next to it.

The pass rate that decides each step comes from an eval set; we wrote about that in write the evals before the prompt. For how we set approvals and permissions on a build, see how we work and trust and security.

Questions buyers ask

How much autonomy should an AI agent have at launch? Less than you think it can handle. Start with tight approval gates, run the agent in a shadow lane against your team for one to two weeks, and loosen one threshold at a time as the measured pass rate supports it.

What should an AI agent never do without approval? Anything you can’t undo, and anything above a limit your business already uses, such as a dollar amount or a confidence score. Write that list before you give the agent any tools.

How do you set approval rules for an AI agent? Express each rule as a number your team already understands and keep it in configuration, not code. Then changing a rule is a settings change, not a rebuild.

What happens when an AI agent is confidently wrong? Plan for it before launch: who notices, how fast, how much it can affect, and how you undo it. Log every action with its inputs, reasoning and who authorised it, so any action can be traced and reversed.
